faq.q: How does salt pull water out of microbes?
faq.a: By osmosis. Water moves through a cell membrane from where there is more water to where there is less, so in very salty surroundings water leaves the microbe's cell and it dries out.
asks: Why does salt dry things out?

faq.a: Strong salting stops most bacteria growing and kills some, but a few kinds, called halophiles, love salt. That is why salted food is often dried or kept cool as well.

faq.q: Why does honey last so long?
faq.a: Honey is about four-fifths sugar and less than a fifth water, and it is slightly acidic. Microbes that land in it lose water and cannot grow, so sealed honey keeps for years.
Traditional jam is over half sugar. All that sugar ties up the water so moulds and bacteria cannot grow, which is why sealed jam keeps for months.
asks: Why does jam need so much sugar?

faq.q: What other ways do people keep food without a fridge?
faq.a: Drying, smoking, pickling in vinegar, fermenting, canning and keeping food cold in cellars. Each makes life hard for microbes by removing water, adding acid or heat, or keeping things cold.
asks: How was food kept before fridges?

facts: Salt and sugar preserve food by drawing water out of microbes through osmosis.
Honey is usually about 17 to 18 percent water, too little for most microbes to grow.
Some microbes, called halophiles, thrive in very salty places such as salt lakes.
